newsitem.title: UK: Aide to Major tried to influence probe - papers.
newsitem.headline: Aide to Major tried to influence probe - papers.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major seemed to be in more trouble on Sunday when newspapers reported that a senior aide had tried to influence a probe into a corruption allegation after it broke two years ago.

The Sunday Telegraph and three other broadsheet papers said David Willetts had sent a confidential memorandum in 1994 to senior members of the ruling Conservative party outlining ways in which the investigation could be halted or toned down.
The so-called "cash for questions" affair is shaping up to be one of the worst scandals to hit the Conservatives, widely accused by opponents of sleaze after 17 years in power.

The suggestion that the Conservatives tried to influence the course of an independent parliamentary probe -- seen as a grave breach of procedure -- will spell more grief for Major at a time when he is trying to stop his party feuding over Britain's role in the European Union.
The opposition Labour party, with a commanding lead in the opinion polls, has already vowed to press Major over the affair when parliament reopens on October 14.

The four newspapers said Willetts, now Paymaster-General, had written the memo after talking to the Conservative head of a parliamentary committee charged with investigating the affair, which involved former junior trade minister Neil Hamilton.

Hamilton resigned in 1994 after he was accused of accepting money from Mohammed al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of London's luxury Harrods store, in return for tabling a series of questions in parliament.
Hamilton dropped a libel case against the Guardian newspaper on the eve of the trial last week in which Major and deputy premier Michael Hesletine had been called as witnesses.
The Sunday Telegraph said the Willetts memo suggested that investigation chairman Sir Geoffrey Johnson-Smith be asked to hold off until Hamilton's libel action was over.
Willetts also said the government could use the Conservative majority on the committee to minimise the inquiry's scope.

The committee eventually rapped Hamilton' knuckles for not declaring he had received free hotel accommodation in Paris but decided not to hear the bulk of the evidence until the libel action had been settled.

"He (Johnson-Smith) could: A, argue now sub judice and get committee to set it aside or B, investigate it as quickly as possible, exploiting good Tory (Conservative) majority. We are inclined to go for A, but he wants our advice," the Sunday Times quoted the memo as saying.

Johnson-Smith acknowledged talking to Willetts and said the conversation had not had any influence on the probe. But he told the Observer newspaper: "I would not be surprised if I gave the impression to Mr Willetts that there were some options."
Hamilton admitted accepting payments totalling 10,000 pounds ($15,600) from lobbyist Ian Greer, who also gave money to about 30 other predominantly Conservative members of parliament.
Saturday's Guardian newspaper said Hamilton had misled senior ministers when they questioned him over the allegations.

Major has agreed to cooperate fully with a new investigation by parliament's Commissioner for Standards. A spokesman for Major's office said on Saturday the government did not want to prejudge that investigation and had nothing to add.
